finding.claim: Unauthenticated remote command injection in GET /ping: the unvalidated query parameter `host` is concatenated into a shell command string passed to exec(), so a request such as /ping?host=127.0.0.1;id runs arbitrary shell commands as the server process user.
finding.source: req.query.host (tools.js:7), attacker-controlled HTTP query string on an unauthenticated route
finding.sink: child_process.exec("ping -c 1 " + req.query.host) (tools.js:7), which runs the string through /bin/sh

trace.note: app.get("/ping") registers an unauthenticated route; no auth middleware is installed anywhere in the file
req.query.host is read and string-concatenated into the command; exec() invokes a shell, so ;, &&, |, backticks and $() are interpreted
stdout of the injected command is returned in the HTTP response, so output is directly readable by the attacker
app.listen(3001) binds to all interfaces by default, so the route is reachable from the network, not only localhost

finding.guards_checked: No input validation or allowlist on req.query.host (no regex, no IP/hostname parsing); no escaping (shell quoting or shell-free spawn with an args array); not using execFile/spawn with an argument array (contrast /version at line 16, which does use execFile with fixed args); no authentication or authorization middleware; no rate limiting. Express's query parser can deliver host as an array (?host=a&host=b), which is also concatenated and does not stop injection. Precondition: none beyond network reachability of port 3001.

verdict.guard_found: none. tools.js:7 concatenates req.query.host directly into the exec() string with no validation, escaping, or execFile/spawn argument array. The only other file-level control is tools.js:9-10, which just returns 502 on error and does not block injection. There is no auth middleware anywhere in tools.js (tools.js:4-28). The safe execFile call at tools.js:16 is on a different route.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous: the GET /ping route at tools.js:6 has no auth, and req.query.host at tools.js:7 is concatenated into a string passed to exec(), which runs it through /bin/sh, so ;-separated commands execute and stdout is returned at tools.js:11. app.listen(3001) at tools.js:28 binds to all interfaces by default, so the route is network-reachable.

finding.claim: All routes are unauthenticated and the server listens on all interfaces, so every endpoint (/ping, /version, /uptime) is exposed to any network client. This is a precondition that makes CMDI-1 remotely exploitable and also exposes host information.
finding.sink: app.listen(3001) (tools.js:28) with no host argument, and route handlers at lines 6, 15 and 24 with no auth checks

trace.note: listen(3001) with no host argument binds 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces)
/version has no auth and returns the git HEAD of the server's working directory
/uptime has no auth and returns host uptime and load output

finding.guards_checked: No authentication, authorization, IP allowlist, or localhost-only binding anywhere in the file. No reverse-proxy or middleware configuration is present in this directory, so none can be verified from this code alone.
finding.repro: curl 'http://<host>:3001/uptime' and curl 'http://<host>:3001/version' return data with no credentials.

verdict.guard_found: none. tools.js has no auth, authorization, IP allowlist, or host-restricted listen. The only listen call is app.listen(3001) at tools.js:28, which has no host argument. Routes at tools.js:6, 15, and 24 have no checks. No middleware or proxy config exists in the directory (Glob returned only tools.js).
verdict.reason: Anonymous network clients can reach /version (tools.js:15-21, returns git HEAD) and /uptime (tools.js:24-26, returns uptime output) because app.listen(3001) at tools.js:28 has no host argument and no route has an auth check, so the finding holds as an unauthenticated information-disclosure and exposure issue. Severity is low on its own, and the /version repro only works if the server's working directory is a git repo (otherwise it returns 500 at tools.js:18).
